sub_answers.sub_question: How can disorder, finite-size effects, and nonuniversal edge chemistry mimic or obscure topological spin-response signatures?
sub_answers.text: Local disorder can reconstruct edge states in the Brillouin zone and thus change where and how spin-response appears at the boundary, potentially mimicking or obscuring topological signals [d35445s0p0]. Finite-size effects (width and length) modify edge-state properties and their detectability, altering spin-response signatures tied to edges [d35445s0p0]. Edge modifications that tune direction- and spin-dependent Fermi velocities can shift or reshape spectral spin features that one might ascribe to topology [d35445s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In what ways do interaction-driven collective modes produce spectral features that confound topological interpretations?
sub_answers.text: Electron-electron interactions can turn single-particle edge excitations into spin-like zero-energy states while gapping out single-particle charge excitations, changing the spectral character of boundary responses [d78351s0p0]. Above a critical interaction strength edge quasiparticles can lose coherence and merge with bulk states, erasing spectral edge signatures that could be mistaken for topological transitions [d78351s0p0]. Collective modes in topological materials can also show spin-charge separation and strong phonon-plasmon hybridisation, producing spin- or charge-like collective excitations that complicate attribution to single-particle topology [d38628s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What limitations arise from finite experimental resolution, substrate coupling, and overlapping phonon or charge excitations?
How robust are proposed spin-susceptibility topological markers against model assumptions and parameter variations?
sub_answers.text: Topological markers based on correlations can remain robust against finite dephasing up to a finite threshold, implying they are not immediately destroyed by weak noise [d109548s0p0]. Strong real-space disorder induces transitions between topological and Anderson insulating phases but systems near the critical point still show finite robustness to dephasing, indicating sensitivity to disorder strength and model parameters [d109548s0p0]. Edge-state properties and hence spin-response markers depend on geometric parameters (width and length) and on edge modifications, so markers vary with these model assumptions and parameter choices [d35445s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What experimental techniques measure frequency-dependent spin response (e.g., ESR, inelastic neutron scattering, spin-polarized EELS)?
sub_answers.text: Electron spin resonance (ESR) directly measures frequency-dependent spin response [d49951s0p0]. Inelastic neutron scattering probes the dynamical spin susceptibility and collective spin-wave excitations [d16649s0p0]. Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and optical pump–probe / pump–THz spectroscopy have been used to access spin and collective excitation spectra in correlated and low-dimensional systems [d16649s0p0][d44195s0p0][d35252s0p0].

What is dynamic spin susceptibility and how is it defined in frequency and momentum space?
What are 2D Dirac systems and which materials are canonical examples?
sub_answers.text: Two-dimensional (2D) Dirac systems are electronic systems whose low-energy quasiparticles are described by a linear (Dirac) dispersion relation in two dimensions, i.e. massless Dirac electrons with conical bands near Dirac points [d26823s0p0][d44189s0p0]. Graphene-like materials realize such Dirac band structures in a 2D lattice and can host Dirac cones at opposite momenta [d26823s0p0]. Topological-insulator surfaces are an experimental realization of massless 2D Dirac electrons, as observed for Bi2Se3 surface states [d44189s0p0].

How do bulk band inversions and gap openings in Dirac models modify spin response functions?

How do electron–electron interactions and disorder alter calculated dynamic spin susceptibility in 2D Dirac systems?
sub_answers.text: Electron-electron interactions can renormalize and stabilize a metallic phase in 2D electron systems, altering the computed spin susceptibility quantitatively through many-body effects [d138078s0p0]. Near a disorder-driven metal–insulator quantum critical point, the density of states of collective modes diverges and causes critical thermodynamic behavior including an anomalous enhancement of the spin susceptibility as the transition is approached [d138642s0p0]. Practical many-body calculations of interaction-induced renormalization of the spin susceptibility in realistic 2D systems have been performed using the leading-order "ladder-bubble" expansion with dynamically screened Coulomb interactions [d138078s0p0].

How can random impurities, sample size-dependent quantization, and chemically modified or reconstructed sample edges produce signals in spin-resolved probes that imitate or hide signatures attributed to topological edge states?
sub_answers.text: Local disorder and impurities can reconstruct edge states in momentum space, shifting or redistributing their spectral weight and thereby producing or masking spin-resolved signals that would be attributed to topological edges [d35445s0p0]. Magnetic fields or impurity-induced breaking of time-reversal symmetry open gaps and enable backscattering that modifies edge transport and spin responses, which can hide or alter signatures of helical edge modes [d64314s0p0]. Finite sample width and length change the spatial extent and energy quantization of edge channels, producing size-dependent spectra that can imitate or obscure topological quantization in spin-resolved probes [d35445s0p0]. Chemical modification or reconstruction of edges can make edge-mode velocities spin- and direction-dependent or relocate edge channels along different edges, producing altered spin-resolved features that mimic or hide pristine topological-edge signals [d35445s0p0][d12543s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which interaction-driven collective excitations (e.g., magnons, spinon continua, charge-density-wave amplitude modes) generate peaks or continua in single-particle and two-particle spectra that could be mistaken for topological edge or surface states, and what distinguishing energy, momentum, or temperature dependencies do they show?

What quantitative errors or ambiguities are introduced by limited energy or momentum resolution, mechanical and electronic coupling to typical substrates (e.g., SiO2, hBN, metallic backplanes), and nearby phonon or plasmon modes when extracting topological spin-response features from tunneling, neutron, or Raman measurements?

To what extent do commonly used microscopic assumptions (noninteracting approximations, mean-field order parameters, ideal edge terminations) and variations in key parameters (disorder strength, interaction U, spin-orbit coupling λ, chemical potential μ, finite sample width) change predicted spin-susceptibility signatures claimed to be topological?
sub_answers.text: Interaction effects can gap or reconstruct surface and edge states so that mean-field or noninteracting predictions of spin response are qualitatively altered by interactions [d12628s0p0]. Disorder strength strongly affects whether backscattering is present or suppressed and can reconstruct edge spectral weight, changing predicted spin-susceptibility signatures [d35445s0p0][d64314s0p0]. Finite sample width and geometry redistribute edge channels and can change the apparent quantization or location of spin-response features compared with idealized terminations [d35445s0p0][d12543s0p0]. Even when bulk response terms (e.g. a non-quantized θ-term) vary, one-dimensional edge channels can still yield quantized transport, showing that bulk-based approximations can misattribute or miss edge spin-related signals [d12543s0p0]. Interactions can change the character of low-energy boundary excitations (for example, turning charge edge modes into spin-like zero-energy excitations), altering single-particle and spin-response spectra relative to noninteracting expectations [d78351s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which experimental probes provide frequency-resolved measurements of the spin susceptibility S(q,ω) or χ(ω) — list specific techniques (inelastic neutron scattering, electron spin resonance/ESR, spin-polarized electron energy-loss spectroscopy, resonant inelastic x-ray scattering/RIXS, Raman scattering, terahertz absorption, Brillouin light scattering, spin-polarized STM, muon spin rotation) and note for each the typical energy/frequency range, momentum resolution, and what component of the spin response (longitudinal vs transverse, local vs q-dependent) they directly measure?

For pump–probe and terahertz (THz) spectroscopies applied to two-dimensional magnetic or spin-orbit-coupled materials (e.g., monolayer/crystal flakes like CrI3, FePS3, transition-metal dichalcogenides, kagome or Kitaev candidates), how are time-domain observables (transient Kerr/Faraday rotation, time-resolved MOKE, THz conductivity/absorption, pump-driven spin precession) converted into dynamic spin susceptibility χ(ω) or χ''(ω)? Specify typical pump parameters, probe frequencies, temporal resolution needed, analysis methods (Fourier transforms, fitting to damped oscillator models, two-temperature or Bloch-equation fits), and examples where these yielded χ(ω) in 2D materials.

What experimentally distinguishable features in frequency- and momentum-resolved spin-response data should one expect for topological magnetic or spin-liquid phases versus conventional (trivial) ordered magnets — e.g., presence of broad fractionalized continua vs sharp magnon peaks, gapless edge-mode spectral weight, spinon band thresholds or continuum edges, chiral magnon resonances related to nonzero Chern number, polarization- and q-dependence signatures, and characteristic energy scales and linewidth differences to use as diagnostics?

What are the typical sample preparation and measurement conditions required to obtain reliable frequency-dependent spin-response data: sample forms and sizes (large single crystals vs exfoliated monolayers, required scattering volume for INS or RIXS, surface preparation for EELS/STM), encapsulation/substrate choices (hBN, suspended), base temperatures (mK, <1 K, few K, tens of K depending on gap/ordering temperature), magnetic field strengths and orientations (zero-field, small fields for splitting, Tesla-range for ESR/INS), cryostat/vacuum requirements, and signal-to-noise considerations (integration times, repeated pumping, required sample uniformity)?

Provide a clear definition of the dynamical (frequency- and momentum-dependent) spin susceptibility: what correlator or response function is used, how is it expressed in Fourier space, and what conventions (retarded/imaginary-time, sign factors) are common?

Describe two-dimensional Dirac electron systems: what band-structure features define them, which materials (e.g., graphene, monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides, bismuthene) are standard textbook examples, and what experimental signatures identify a material as a 2D Dirac system?

Explain how spin–orbit coupling terms enter the low-energy effective Dirac Hamiltonian for 2D crystals: what specific SOC terms (intrinsic/Kane–Mele, Rashba, valley-Zeeman, etc.) appear, how do they modify the Dirac matrix structure, and what material parameters control their magnitudes?

List the typical topological phases that occur in 2D Dirac-based models (quantum spin Hall, Chern insulator, trivial insulator, etc.), and for each give the bulk topological invariant used (Z, Z2, Chern number, spin Chern number) and the physical quantity it counts or protects.

In Dirac-type models with a mass gap or band inversion (for example, due to a tunable Dirac mass term or spin-orbit coupling), how do changes in band ordering and gap magnitude quantitatively affect the spin-spin response (e.g., spectral weight redistribution, resonance shifts, and emergence of gapped vs gapless contributions) at finite momentum and frequency?

For a 2D topological insulator or quantum spin Hall strip, how do localized edge states contribute differently from bulk continuum states to the dynamic (frequency-dependent) spin susceptibility and magnetic response, and what signatures (peaks, continuum thresholds, selection rules) distinguish edge-derived versus bulk-derived spectral features?

When including electron-electron interactions (Hubbard, long-range Coulomb) and nonmagnetic disorder/impurity scattering in 2D Dirac systems, how are predictions for the dynamical spin susceptibility modified — specifically via self-energy and vertex corrections, screening within RPA, lifetime broadening (Born approximation), and possible localization or collective modes?

What are the practical computational routes to obtain the spin susceptibility for a Dirac Hamiltonian: e.g., constructing the retarded spin-spin correlator from Matsubara Green's functions with analytic continuation, evaluating the Kubo bubble and ladder diagrams, using Lehmann representations, and implementing numerical approaches (frequency/momentum integration, Padé or maximum-entropy analytic continuation) to extract Im χ(ω,q) and Re χ(ω,q)?

Which specific forms of disorder (e.g., vacancies, magnetic impurities, edge roughness), finite-size quantization, or chemically modified edges (adsorbates, reconstructed terminations) can generate spin-response signals that imitate or mask signatures attributed to topological edge states, and how do their characteristic spatial and energy scales compare to the expected topological response?

Which interaction-induced collective excitations — such as magnons, spin waves, excitons, Stoner continuum features, or plasmon–spin hybrid modes — produce spectral peaks, gaps, or dispersions that could be misidentified as topological spin-response features, and what experimental observables distinguish these many-body modes from genuine topological signals?

How do finite instrumental energy and momentum resolution, thermal broadening, coupling to a supporting substrate (screening, hybridization), and overlapping phonon or charge-density excitations (optical phonons, charge-order modes) limit the ability to resolve and attribute spin-resolved spectral features to topology rather than conventional quasiparticles?

How sensitive are proposed spin-susceptibility-based topological diagnostics to modeling choices and parameter variations — for example finite-size vs. thermodynamic extrapolation, choice of boundary conditions, strength of spin–orbit and exchange interactions, disorder realization, and numerical convergence — and which parameters most strongly alter the predicted topological markers?
sub_answers.text: Boundary conditions associated with Hermiticity and lattice termination can crucially determine the presence and character of edge states in continuum Dirac descriptions, so choice of boundary condition strongly affects predicted edge response [d56437s0p0]. The system width, length, and strength of edge disorder modify edge-state transport and reconstruction in the Brillouin zone, so finite-size geometry and disorder realizations significantly change predicted signatures [d35445s0p0]. Finite-size effects and moderate interactions can preserve remnant single-particle edge signatures but sufficiently strong interactions or small sizes can destroy quasiparticle coherence and merge edge and bulk states, altering topological markers [d78351s0p0]. Finite device size and coupling to leads can mix bulk and edge contributions (as in Floquet TIs), reducing or changing expected quantized responses and therefore sensitively influencing diagnostics based on spin or transport spectra [d59773s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which laboratory probes and spectroscopic methods can map the energy- and momentum-resolved spin susceptibility (examples to consider: electron spin resonance variants, momentum-resolved inelastic neutron scattering, spin-polarized electron energy-loss spectroscopy, resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, Brillouin light scattering, and ferromagnetic resonance), and what frequency ranges and wavevector resolution does each provide?

In what ways do ultrafast optical pump–probe experiments and time-domain terahertz spectroscopy extract the frequency-dependent spin response in atomically thin magnets and 2D heterostructures (specific mechanisms: impulsive stimulated Raman scattering, transient Kerr/Faraday rotation, THz emission/absorption, and time-resolved MOKE), and what analysis procedures convert measured time traces into dynamic susceptibility χ(ω, q≈0)?

For materials hosting topological spin phases (e.g., spin liquids, quantum anomalous Hall magnets, magnon Chern insulators) versus conventional (trivial) magnetic states, what characteristic features in the spin spectral function should one search for — such as discrete magnon peaks, continuum spectral weight, gapless edge modes, fractionalized spinon continua, or hybridized resonances — and how do their energy scales and linewidths differ?
sub_answers.text: Collective discrete magnon or spin-wave peaks appear in spectroscopic probes such as RIXS and INS as sharp dispersing modes [d7879s0p0][d16649s0p0]. Multi-magnon continua and broader particle-hole spectral weight can coexist with single-magnon features and can mask collective modes in RIXS unless resolution is high [d7879s0p0][d16649s0p0]. Fractionalized spinon continua and a split-off collective “spinon spin wave” mode are signatures of U(1) spinon Fermi-surface spin liquids, with the spin wave splitting from the two-spinon continuum and gauge fluctuations giving power-law weight outside the continuum and a finite lifetime that scales as momentum squared [d49951s0p0]. Electron-spin-resonance and neutron studies can detect resonance modes (e.g., a spin-1 neutron spin resonance) and linewidth/temperature/field dependences such as an ESR linewidth linear in temperature and scaling as B^{2/3} at low temperature in certain spin-liquid scenarios [d42670s0p0][d49951s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are the typical experimental sample requirements and external conditions needed to resolve frequency-dependent spin signals (including sample size, thickness, substrate choice, crystal orientation, surface treatment), and what cryogenic temperatures, static magnetic fields (magnitude and orientation), and vacuum/environmental controls are commonly used to observe sharp resonance or continuum features in 2D magnetic and topological spin systems?

Provide a precise definition of the dynamic (frequency- and momentum-dependent) spin susceptibility: express it as the appropriate two-point spin-spin correlation or retarded Green’s function, show its representation in real time and frequency/momentum space (χ_{ij}(q, ω)), and list common ways to compute it (Kubo formula, Matsubara/analytic continuation, Lehmann representation) including typical units and symmetry constraints.
sub_answers.text: The dynamic (frequency- and momentum-dependent) spin susceptibility is the retarded spin–spin correlation function, defined in real time as χ^R_{ij}(r,t) = -i Θ(t) ⟨[S_i(r,t), S_j(0,0)]⟩ [d84428s0p0][d139414s0p0]. Its frequency- and momentum-space form is χ_{ij}(q,ω) = ∫ dt ∫ d^dr e^{i(ωt - q·r)} χ^R_{ij}(r,t), which admits a Lehmann/spectral representation relating Im χ to the spin spectral function [d84428s0p0][d139414s0p0]. Common computation methods include the Kubo linear-response formula, evaluation on the Matsubara (imaginary-frequency) axis followed by analytic continuation to real frequencies using techniques such as singular-value decomposition, barycentric rational interpolation, or controlled minimal-pole representations, and direct construction from the Lehmann (spectral) representation when eigenstates are available [d139414s0p0][d103773s0p0][d91738s0p0][d84428s0p0]. Symmetry and causality impose constraints such as distinct longitudinal and transverse components, Onsager-Casimir relations and frequency-dependent shifts in response features, and Kramers–Kronig relations connecting real and imaginary parts of χ(ω) [d139414s0p0][d137245s0p0][d29690s0p0].
